about.title: About Trackdown
about.intro: Trackdown is a daily guessing game about the railway. It's a personal hobby project by Bram Gussekloo, made in his spare time: no company, no ads and nothing to buy.
about.gameBody: Every day there's one mystery station. Guess any station and Trackdown draws the fastest train trip from your guess to the mystery: the shorter the trip, the closer you are. You have six guesses.
about.tripsBody: Ahead of time, Trackdown works out from the public timetable the fastest trip from every station to every other one, changes included, and keeps it for the puzzle. That makes the travel times realistic, but simplified: delays, engineering works and today's timetable don't count, so a trip can differ from what a journey planner shows.
about.dataIntro: Trackdown is built on open data. Thanks to the people who publish it.

about.dataGbStations: Station locations: NaPTAN, Department for Transport,
about.dataGbRegions: Regions: ITL1 boundaries, Office for National Statistics, contains OS data © Crown copyright and database right,
about.independentBody: Trackdown is not linked to, or endorsed by, NS, Network Rail or any other railway company. Station and operator names belong to their owners and are only used to describe the real network.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.intro: Trackdown is a personal hobby project, made by one person in their spare time. It is not a company and it doesn't make money. This page explains, in plain words, what happens to your data when you play.
privacy.short1: You don't need an account, a name or an email address to play.
privacy.short2: Your guesses, streak and statistics are stored on your own device.
privacy.short3: Visits are counted anonymously with PostHog. Only if you click Accept does it set a cookie.
privacy.short4: No ads, no advertising cookies, and your data is never sold.
privacy.whoBefore: Trackdown is run by Bram Gussekloo, a private person living in the Netherlands. Under the GDPR (AVG in Dutch) that makes me responsible for the little personal data the site handles. Questions or requests: email
privacy.deviceStorage: To make the game work, Trackdown saves a few things in your browser's local storage: your guesses for each puzzle, from which it works out your streak and statistics, and whether you picked light or dark mode. This never leaves your browser.
privacy.deviceCookies: Two small cookies are needed for the site itself: one keeps your answer in the cookie banner, and one keeps the rail network you picked, if you pick one, so Trackdown opens on it. Both last a year and are only read by Trackdown's own server. Clearing your browser's site data removes all of this and resets your statistics.
privacy.analyticsWhy: I'd like to know how many people play and where they get stuck. For that I use PostHog, an analytics service, on its EU cloud in Frankfurt.
privacy.analyticsCookieless: PostHog counts page views, clicks and game events, such as which guess you're on, whether you solved the puzzle and whether you shared your result. It sets no cookie and can't recognise you on your next visit. Events never contain the stations you guessed, the answer or anything you type. PostHog also sees your browser and device type. Your IP address reaches PostHog with each request, but it is set to throw it away instead of storing it. I do this because I have a legitimate interest in knowing whether the game works.
privacy.analyticsCookieLead: With a cookie, only after Accept.
privacy.analyticsCookie: If you click Accept in the cookie banner, PostHog stores a random ID in a cookie so it can tell returning players apart. The legal basis is your consent. Change your mind at any time with Cookie settings at the bottom of every page; the cookie is then removed.
privacy.analyticsProxy: Analytics travel through t.trackdown.nl, an address PostHog runs for Trackdown on Cloudflare's network. Cloudflare passes the requests on to PostHog and, according to PostHog, keeps no logs of them. It answers from the data centre nearest to you, which is usually, but not always, in the EU.
privacy.analyticsRetention: PostHog never gets your name or email. I keep analytics data for 12 months.
privacy.attestBody: When App Attest is enabled in the iOS app, Apple supplies proof that requests come from a genuine app installation. Trackdown keeps the installation's public key, key identifier and replay counter in Upstash Redis for as long as the registration remains active. One-time enrollment challenges expire after five minutes. These records prevent abuse, do not identify an account, and are not sent to analytics. They are separate from the optional analytics choice.
privacy.serverBody: Like any website, the server that sends you the page sees your IP address, browser, the page you asked for and the time. Trackdown runs on Vercel, in its Frankfurt data centre, which keeps these logs for about an hour to keep the site running and to stop abuse. When you guess a station, its name is sent to the server to work out the train trip; that guess isn't stored or linked to you. Server errors and timings go to PostHog EU so I can fix problems. They never contain your IP address, your guesses or the answer, and are kept for 14 days. I do this because I have a legitimate interest in keeping the game working and safe.
privacy.othersBody: Only the services that make Trackdown run: Vercel for hosting, PostHog for analytics and error logs, Cloudflare, which carries the analytics for PostHog, and Apple and Upstash for iOS App Attest security. Vercel and Cloudflare are American companies, so some data may reach the United States, under the safeguards EU law requires. I don't sell, rent or share your data with anyone else, and I don't use it for advertising.
privacy.rightsBefore: You can ask to see, correct or delete data about you, or object to how it's used. Because there are no accounts, I usually can't tell which data is yours. The easiest way is to decline the cookie and clear your site data. If you'd still like me to look, email
privacy.rightsAfter: and I'll answer within a month. If you're unhappy with how I handle it, you can complain to the Dutch data protection authority, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens.
privacy.changesBody: If Trackdown starts handling data differently, I'll update this page and the date at the top. If the change needs your consent, the cookie banner will ask again.

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.intro: Trackdown is a free game, made for fun by one person. There's no company behind it and nothing to buy. These terms are short on purpose: they keep things fair for you and for me. By playing, you agree to them.
terms.freeBody: Trackdown is offered free of charge and as it is. I do my best to keep a new puzzle up every day, but I can't promise the site is always online, error-free or that your streak survives every update. I may change the game, pause it or stop it, at any time.
terms.plannerTitle: A game, not a journey planner
terms.plannerData: The routes and travel times are built from open data, OVapi GTFS-NL (NDOV, CC0 1.0) and PDOK Bestuurlijke Gebieden (Kadaster, CC BY 4.0) for the Netherlands, and Network Rail SCHEDULE data (CC BY-SA 4.0), NaPTAN and ONS ITL1 boundaries (both Open Government Licence v3.0) for Great Britain, and simplified for the puzzle. They may be out of date or wrong. Please don't plan a real trip with Trackdown; check your train operator's journey planner instead.
terms.plannerIndependent: Trackdown is not linked to, or endorsed by, any railway company. Station and operator names belong to their owners and are only used to describe the real network.
terms.fairBody: Share your results and argue about the answer as much as you like. Please don't scrape the site, flood it with requests, try to break in or get the answer early with tricks, or post today's answer automatically. If someone does, I may block them.
terms.ownBody: The name, design, code and puzzles of Trackdown are mine. The timetable data belongs to its providers and is used under their licence. You may share screenshots and results; please don't copy the game itself.
terms.liabilityBody: As far as Dutch law allows, I'm not liable for any damage from using Trackdown, such as a missed train or a lost streak. Nothing here limits rights you have as a consumer that can't be limited by law.
